issues.legal_issue: The inam grant comprised only the revenue interest and did not include the underlying soil interest.
material_facts: No document recording the original grant or its conditions was produced.
The official inam records described the grant as a concessional revenue payment connected with the temple and recorded only the revenue interest as claimed in the inam inquiry.
Copies of leases suggesting that the grant included the soil interest were tendered without the originals or a foundation for secondary evidence.
The other admissible records did not establish that the soil interest was included in the grant.
issues.conclusion: The grant comprised the melwaram alone, not the kudiwaram.
issues.legal_principle: An inam fair register is an official declaration produced after detailed inquiry and carries supreme importance absent positive and proper contrary evidence. The absence of a presumption that an inam excludes the soil interest does not overcome the evidence in a particular case. Copies of documents are inadmissible as secondary evidence without the required foundation. The Court applied Arunachalam Chetty and Others v. Venkatachalapathi Guruswamigal and considered Venkata v. Sitamadu.

predicates.inam_extent_dispute: The dispute concerns which interests were included in an inam grant.
predicates.official_inam_record_describes_revenue_c: An official inam record describes the grant as a concessional revenue payment and identifies its connection with the relevant institution or service.
predicates.admissible_evidence_of_soil_interest: Admissible evidence establishes that the grant included the underlying soil interest.

issues.definition: When an inam-extent dispute concerns a grant recorded as a revenue concession and admissible evidence does not establish a grant of the soil interest, the grant is treated as including only the revenue interest.

issues.legal_issue: An inam granted to remunerate service attached to a religious institution is not a personal inam and may be resumed when it is alienated.
material_facts: The official records described the inam as a temple endowment for archaka service and recorded the grantees in their capacity as temple officeholders.
The records and a statement by a person enjoying the inam showed that it was treated as remuneration for performing temple services.
The holders alienated the lands, and the Mission possessed them as an alienee.
The inam was not shown to have been granted personally to an individual independently of the temple office.
issues.conclusion: The inam was a service inam, not a personal inam, and its alienation made it liable to resumption.
issues.legal_principle: A grant to an officeholder to remunerate service is a service inam rather than a personal inam, and it is resumable when the service or office conditions are not met. Section 44-B of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926 authorized resumption on specified grounds, including alienation. P. B. Bheemsena Rao v. Sirigiri Paddayella Reddi distinguishes a proper service inam from a personal grant burdened with service; the Court also relied on the records and the earlier treatment of such grants under the Board of Revenue's Standing Order Rule 54.

predicates.service_inam_dispute: The dispute concerns whether an inam granted in connection with institutional service may be resumed.
predicates.grant_attached_to_temple_office: The grant records or other evidence connect the inam to service performed through a temple office rather than to the grantee personally.
predicates.service_grant_alienated: The holder or a successor transferred the inam or the land interest covered by it.

issues.definition: When an inam is attached to a temple office and is alienated, the service inam is treated as resumable.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory resumption scheme was within the legislature's competence and was not invalid because its operation restored an endowment's lost benefit or because title deeds had been validated by legislation.
material_facts: The resumption provision concerned inams connected with religious or charitable endowments and dealt with land tenures and land revenue administration.
The provision was enacted under the earlier constitutional arrangements and later amended, while a corresponding provision was enacted under a later statute.
The relevant parliamentary legislation validated inam title deeds but did not create a contract between the government and inam holders.
Resumption and regrant restored to the temple a benefit it had lost through alienation.
issues.conclusion: The resumption provision and its amendment were within legislative competence, the title-deed legislation did not bar resumption, and restoring the benefit did not impermissibly advantage a denominational institution.
issues.legal_principle: The provincial powers over land tenures, land revenue administration, and religious and charitable endowments, considered together, supported comprehensive legislation concerning inams. Under rule 4 of the Devolution Rules, the Governor-General in Council's decision on whether a subject was provincial would have been final; section 292 of the Government of India Act, 1935 sustained the earlier provision, and the later legislature had corresponding authority. The legislation validating title deeds cured defects in their execution but created no contract or immunity from resumption for breach of grant conditions. Resumption and regrant that merely restore a benefit lost by an endowment do not put that institution at an advantage.

predicates.inam_resumption_law_challenge: A party challenges the validity of a law authorizing resumption of inams connected with religious or charitable institutions.
predicates.law_concerns_land_tenures_and_revenue_an: The law regulates land tenures and revenue in connection with religious or charitable endowments.
predicates.title_validation_only_cured_deed_defects: The legislation relied on to validate grants cured defects in title documents without creating a contract or an immunity from the grant's conditions.
predicates.resumption_restores_lost_endowment_benef: The resumption and regrant return to an endowment a benefit it had lost through a transfer.

issues.definition: A challenged resumption law is treated as valid when it concerns land and revenue in connection with endowments, validating legislation only cured deed defects, and resumption restores a lost endowment benefit.

issues.legal_issue: Long possession does not bar the government's resumption of a revenue interest when no limitation period governs the relevant exercise of governmental authority.
material_facts: The Mission had possessed the lands for many years as an alienee.
The resumption concerned the melwaram alone.
No law prescribed a period within which the government had to exercise its authority to impose assessment on land liable to public revenue.
issues.conclusion: The Mission's adverse-possession claim did not prevent resumption.
issues.legal_principle: There is no period of limitation within which the government must exercise its prerogative to impose assessment on land liable to public revenue. The Court applied Boddapalli Jagannadham v. Secretary of State and Subramaniam Chettiar v. Secretary of State.

predicates.government_revenue_interest_resumption_d: The dispute concerns the government's resumption or assessment of a revenue interest in land.
predicates.resumption_concerns_revenue_interest: The interest resumed is the revenue interest rather than the underlying soil interest.
predicates.no_limitation_period_governs_government_: No applicable law sets a time limit for the government's exercise of authority to impose assessment on the land.

issues.definition: When the government resumes a revenue interest and no limitation period governs its assessment authority, long possession does not bar the resumption.
